jim-winget-alias-jim-cason-1890-08-12.A1: A NEGRO LYNCHED.—The Caucasian was informed by a reliable gentleman that Jim Winget, alias Jim Cason, was lynched Tuesday night in Bossier parish by parties unknown. It is stated that Wingett was a witness in the murder case in which N. H. Wyche is accused of killing a young man named Smith, near Plain Dealing. It is also stated that Winget was indirectly connected in the homicide. It is a fact, however, that Winget was taken from his house, on the H. D. Kelly place in Bassier and carried one and a half miles away and hung in Wyche's yard.—Shreveport Caucasian, 15th.
jim-winget-alias-jim-cason-1890-08-12.A2: Gov. Nicholls has offered $250 reward for the apprehension of Nat H. Wyche, who murdered W. R. Hollman, in this parish, on July 9, 1890.

Cowhided by White Caps.
on Baxter colored and Mrs.
John Baxter, colored, and Mrs. Jennie Smith, white, have been living together lately at Smithfield, Pa. Awhite cap warning for them to quit the community was recently received by them, to which they paid no attention. Last Monday night Baxter was called to his door, where he was confronted by ten masked men carrying cowhides. He fought pluckily but was overpowered and beaten unmercifully.
john-baxter-smithfield-1890-08-04.A3:
"White Caps" With Cowhides.
Uniontown, Pa., August 16.—John Baxter, colored, and Mrs. Jennie Smith, white, have been living together at Smithfield late-ly, and had taken possession of the house of Baxter's old father, driving the aged man out of home and compelling him to sleep in barns. Recently the guilty pair received a notice signed "White Caps," warning them to quit the community or take the consequences. Baxter thought he knew the writer of the notice and he wrote on the back of it as follows and mailed it to the party: "Come on. I dare you to come," and signed it "Texas John." The next thing Baxter heard of the matter was a rap at his door, which aroused him from his midnight slumbers, and presently he was confronted by eight or ten stalwart men, well masked, each with a cowhide in his hand. Mrs. Smith had heeded the warning and fled, but the invaders doubled the dose on her paramour, administering to him one of the most terrible beatings ever heard of in this community. He fought a plucky fight, but was overpowered by numbers.

onancock-onancock-1890-08-17.A1:
WHITES AND NEGROES FIGHT.
Stones, Clubs and Pistols Used With
Serious Results on a Steamer.
There was a riot between whites and negroes on the steamboat Helen yesterday at Onancock, Va., in which one man was shot and badly wounded and a number of others seriously hurt from blows on the head with stones and clubs. The Helen left Baltimore Saturday night with four hundred negroes, including some of the toughest characters in Baltimore, for the big negro camp meeting at Onancock, Va. The trip down the river was a quiet one, although the darkies drank considerable whisky. Sunday was a big day at the camp. In the afternoon, just as the darkies were filing on board the steamer for the return trip, a party of white men on the wharf got into a disturbance with half a dozen of the negroes. Before the captain or other officers of the boat realized the situation a general fight was in progress.

Pistols were fired and volleys of stones filled the air. The negroes became wild and utterly unmanageable. They smashed the steamer chairs and hurled the pieces at the whites on the wharf, who in turn sent stones flying through the cabin and saloon windows. One negro was shot through the right shoulder and two others had their heads split open by stones. A number of other heads were cracked. Several of the white men were slightly hurt. When the steamer arrived in Baltimore the negroes hustled off and hurried away. No arrests were made. Capt. Smith of the Helen says that if he had not cut the ropes and hurried away from the wharf the result would, no doubt, have been more serious.

A special dispatch from Onancock says: "The trouble grew out of the bad conduct of the negroes, who had been drinking heavily. As they passed through a crowd of whites on their way to the boat they jostled and swore at them and one negro grossly insulted a young white girl. The words were scarcely out of his mouth when a blow from a stalwart young man sent him sprawling to the deck, and then the whole crowd joined in the row."

onancock-onancock-1890-08-17.A3:
A NEGRO OUTRAGE.
DRUNKEN COLORED EXCURSIONISTS
FIRE ON WHITE PEOPLE.
They Create Pandemonium on a Steamer and Wherever They Go-Sunday Desecration.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
Dracony. Your Amount 18. About
ONANCOCK, VA., August 18.—About four hundred colored excursionists from Baltimore arrived here yesterday morning on the steamer Helen, Captain Smith, of the Eastern Shore Line, to attend the colored Methodist camp-meeting now going on at Savageville, two miles south of Onancock. The steamer was chartered for the occasion by a committee of colored men, at the head of which was Philip Finney, formerly of Accomac.

FIRE-WATER FLOWED FREELY.

On their way down the bay Saturday night many of the excursionists were under the influence of liquor and made things lively on board the steamer. A bar-room was in operation on the boat and liquor flowed freely among the excursionists.

THE LEADER ATTACKED.

Just before they reached Crisfield some of the machinery about the steamer broke and several of the drunken and infuriated negroes laid the blame of the accident on Philip Finney and swore they would throw him into the bay, but Finney escaped from them and took refuge in the pilot-house.

On arriving at the camp-grounds some of them became involved in several rows, in which clubs, knives, and razors were freely used, and three or four were cut and painfully bruised.

WHITE PEOPLE ON THE WHARF.

Most of the excursionists returned to Onancock in the afternoon to take the steamer back to Baltimore. There were, about fifteen or twenty white persons at the wharf. About the time the steamer was to leave a drunken negro attempted to pull a white boy off one of the piles on the wharf. Several white men went to the assistance of the boy, and the negro was taken in hand by his friends and carried on board the steamer.

THE WHITES ATTACKED.

At this some of the negroes on the upper deck began to curse and abuse the white men in an outrageous manner. A young white man struck at one of the negroes on the boat with a cane, whereupon the negroes began to throw canes, chairs, and other missiles at the white men on the wharf, and several of the negroes drew pistols and began to fire at the white people, among whom were many small children.

THE WHITES UNARMED.

The white men were unarmed and unprepared for a difficulty, but many of them seized brick-bats and shot the steamer left the wharf as soon as possible. The negroes kept up their cursing and shooting till the steamer was more than a hundred yards from the wharf.

INTENSE EXCITEMENT.

When the affair became known in the town the most intense excitement prevailed and it was very fortunate for the negroes that the steamer left the wharf before the people of the town were informed of it.

Mayor Taylor, of Onancock, telegraphed to the Chief of Police of Baltimore to arrest the ringleaders of the difficulty on the arrival of the steamer in Baltimore this morning.

A SHARBY SET.

Most of the excursionists were shabby and ill-mannered, and cursed Captain Smith and insulted other officers on the boat. The boat left here in such a burry that more than one hundred of the excursionists were left behind.

A Cambridge correspondent of the Baltimore Sun, says; Dorchester county has no candidate for Congress this year, but even with this local interest eliminated politicians and people generally are watching all the moves. An active contest is going on here, however, between the friends of Colonel Henry Page, of Somerset and Congressman Gibson. The friends of the two gentlemen seem about equally divided. One of the local Democratic papers has espoused the cause of Mr. Gibson, and the other that of Colonel Page. In Cambridge, East New Market and Vienna districts the indications are that a contest will be had unless a compromise by a division of delegates between the two candidates is effected beforehand. In the other districts the chances are there will be no contest, but the fight for their votes will be made at Cambridge on the day of the convention by appeals to the delegates. The primaries will take place on Saturday, 23d instant, and the convention will meet on the Tuesday following.

A NEGRO OUTRAGE.
Drunken Colored Excursionists From Baltimore Ralse a Row and Fire Upon Inoffending White People in Accomac County.
ONANCOCK, VA., August 19.—About four hundred colored excursionists, from Baltimore, arrived here yesterday morning on the steamer Helen, Captain Smith, of the Eastern Shore line, to attend the colored Methodist camp-meeting now going on at Savageville, two miles south of Onancock. The steamer was chartered for the occasion by a committee of colored men, at the head of which was Phillip Finney, formerly of Accomac. On their way down the bay Saturday night, many of the excursionists were under the influence of liquor, and made things lively on board the steamer. A barroom was in operation on the boat and liquor flowed freely.

Just before they reached Crisfield some of the machinery about the steamer broke and several of the drunken and infuriated negroes laid the blame of the accident on Phillip Finney and swore they would throw him into the bay, but Finney escaped from them and took refuge in the pilot-house.

On arriving at the camp-grounds some of them became involved in several rows, in which clubs, knives, and razors were freely used, and three or four were cut and painfully bruised.

Most of the excursionists returned to Onancock in the afternoon, to take the steamer back to Baltimore. There were about fifteen or twenty white persons at the wharf. About the time the steamer was to leave, a drunken negro attempted to pull a white boy off one of the piles on the wharf. Several white men went to the assistance of the boy, and the negro was taken in hand by his friends and carried on board the steamer.

At this some of the negroes on the upper deck began to curse and abuse the white men in an outrageous manner. A young white man struck at one of the negroes on the boat with a cane, whereupon the negroes began to throw canes, chairs, and other missiles at the white men on the wharf, and several of the negroes drew pistols and began to fire at the white people, among whom were many children.

The white men were unarmed and unprepared for a difficulty, but many of them seized brick-bats and let them fly at the negroes, knocking some down and smashing several windows on the upper deck. The town sergeant, who was on the wharf, did what he could to stop the difficulty, but the negroes grew more and more violent and kept up a steady fire on the white men, who were forced to find shelter behind piles of plank and brick on the wharf.

American Bar Association. SARATOGA, Aug. 22.—At the American Bar Association this morning officers were elected as follows: President, Simeon E. Baldwin, of New Haven: secretary, Edward Otis Hinckley, of Baltimore; treasurer, Francis Rawle, of Philadelphia; executive committee, the president, secretary, treasurer, Henry Hitchcock, George A. Mercer of Georgia, W. P. Walls of Michigan, and Alfred Hemenway of Massachusetts. A vice-president for each State and a local council for each State were also elected. Ex-Judge Dillon read a report of the committee on obtaining increase of the salaries of federal judges, recommending that the association continue to urge that the salaries be increased, and that all the bar associations in the United States be invited to co-operate with the American Bar Association in continuing to urge favorable action of Congress. War-Ship Gunners Killed. SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 22.—The steamer Oceanic arrived this afternoon, twenty-two days from Hong Kong, thirteen from Yokohama. On July 31 the United States flagship Omaha returned to Yokohama from target practice outside of the bay, and reported that Carl Emanuelson, leader, and J. E. Kirk, of Baltimore, sponger, had been killed by a premature discharge from a Dahlgren gun. Kirke was blown from the vessel and the remains could not be found. Emanuelson was terribly mangled. Victims of the Old Colony Accident.
BOSTON, Aug. 22.—The reports from the Quincy Hospital to-night are more favorable than at any time since the accident. Little Elizabeth Fenely was to-day able to take a little nourishment, and that was considered a most favorable sign. Captain Abbott has improved a little, and Lucy Johnson, the Fenely's colored nurse, has been promised that she can sit up in a few days. Rev. F. M. Dimmick and his wife, of Los Angeles, Cal., are very low, but there are some chances of their recovery.

Another Body Found in the Car-Depot Wreck.

Another Body Found in the Car-Depot Wreck.

PHILADELPHIA, Aug. 22.—The search of the ruins of the street-car depot wrecked by the wind last night, was continued throughout the night. This morning the body of John Christy, who was reported lost, was found crushed beneath a pile of bricks. No more bodies have been found, and it is believed the five already taken out will complete the list of the killed. The loss to the company is estimated at $30,000.

Col. Dudley's Libel Suit Dismissed.

NEW YORK, Aug. 22.—Judge Beach has entered an order in the Supreme Court discontinuing the action brought by Col. Wm. Dudley to recover damages from George Jones as treasurer of the Times Publishing Company for alleged libel in publishing the alleged "Blocks-of-Five" letter. The order was entered by consent of counsel.

Capture of a Kentucky Desperado.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., Aug. 22.—Capt. Gaither, of the company which is protecting Judge Lilly's court at Hazard, Perry county, reports that Joe Davidson, leader of the French faction in the French-Eversole feud, has been captured. He says Davidson is the worst desperado of all, and his capture has struck terror into the lawless bands.

Colored Boy Lynched.

NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 22.—The Picayune's Baton Rouge special reports the lynching of Willis Alexander, colored, aged seventeen, in that parish, last night. Alexander was accused of having attempted to assault an eleven-year-old white girl. His body was found to-day hanging from a tree by the roadside.

being reprimanded by her father on the 21st Carrie Walker, 17 years old, living in St. Louis, went into her room and swallowed a dose of arsenic, dying an hour afterwards.

The Thousand Island Park Hotel and twenty cottages at Thousand Island Park, on the St. Lawrence river, were burned on the morning of the 21st. Loss, $150,000.

An explosion of powder at the Standard Cartridge Company's works, four miles south of Blue Island, Ill., on the 21st resulted in the killing of one man and the injury of twenty men, boys and girls.

By the blowing down of street railway sheds at Philadelphia on the 21st, four persons were killed outright and several others were fatally injured.

Five members of a pleasure party were drowned by the upsetting of their boat off Whitestown L. I., on the 21st.

Masked burglars entered the residence of Michael Shelby, a farmer residing near Wooster, O., on the 21st and bound and gagged the family and stole $4,000.

By the collision of a freight and passenger train at Carbondale, Ill., on the Illinois Central road on the 21st Charles Mitchell, the freight conductor, was killed.

B. H. Cooks & Co., clothing merchants of Nashville, Tenn., made an assignment on the 21st. Liabilities, $200,000; assets, $140,000.

The Blue Grass Palace Exposition was opened at Creston, Ia., on the 21st by Governor Boies.
THE Blue Grass Palace Exposition was opened at Creston, Ia., on the 21st by Governor Boies.

At Cassopolis, Mich., on the morning of the 21st James Matthews killed Mrs. John Matthews for refusing to marry him. He then shot himself in the head, inflicting a fatal wound.

A freight train on the Missouri, Kansas & Texas railroad telescoped a passenger train at Paola, Mo., on the 21st, killing Pullman Conductor Camp and seriously injuring Engineer Woodward.

It was said on the 22d that great destitution prevailed among the farmers in Aparahoe, County, Col., and that between 500 and 800 people were in a starving condition, the entire failure of crops being given as the cause.

SEVKRE frosts were reported in Minnesota, North Dakota and Manitoba on the 22d, and fears were entertained that great damage had been done to crops.

WILLIAM ALEXANDER, a 17-year-old mulatto, was lynched near Baton Rouge, La., on the 22d for attempted assault on a 11-year-old white girl.

The special agent sent to Oklahoma by Secretary of the Interior Noble returned on the 22d and confirmed the stories of destitution existing there and said help should be sent at once.

A car on the Mount Penn Gravity railroad at Reading, Pa., ran away on the 22d with eighteen passengers on board, making the descent in three minutes, and rolled down a fifty-foot embankment at the end of the track. Four persons were killed, two fatally and others seriously injured.

In jumping from an engine that had become unmanageable on the Denver, Utah & Pacific railroad near Lyons, Col., on the 22d three men were killed and others seriously hurt.

About 200 engineers, firemen and switchmen employed by the Union Stock Yards Switching Association of Chicago struck on the 22d for an increase in wages and more rest on Sundays.

The business failures throughout the country during the seven days ended on the 22d number 192, as compared with 197 the preceding week and 200 for the corresponding week last year.

The air-brakes of a freight train standing on a grade at Summit, Cal., gave way on the 22d and the train dashed into another freight train at Cascade, killing four men.

Two young men were killed by the premature discharge of a cannon in a sham battle at Athens, Pa., on the 22d.

People in Northwest Wyoming were excited on the 22d over rich finds of gold in the Tongue river field and there was a stampede from the surrounding country.

Fire at Groten, S. D., on the 22d destroyed nearly all the west half of the business portion of the town, entailing a loss of $150,000.

In a trotting match for $5,000 at Washington Park, Chicago, on the 22d Palo Alto defeated Jack in three straight heats, the last being made in 2:13, the fastest time on record in a match.
NEAR Shelbyville, Mich., on the 22d a Barnum & Bailey circus train broke in two. A car platform was torn out, and two men were thrown under the wheels and killed.
